limbs.label: Conscious, deliberate dishonesty attributable to the successful party
Court deception and materiality / operative cause
Critical undermining of process and powerful probability of real injustice

rubric.mapping: Each limb is an internal evidence-readiness score from 0 to 50. 0 = no supporting material; 10 = lead or unsupported inference; 20 = documented anomaly or indirect/circumstantial support; 25 = minimum internal gate with a particularised case and credible primary-source support for that limb; 30–40 = stronger authenticated primary material and corroboration; 50 = complete, admissible, authenticated proof, independently checked and stress-tested. These are triage anchors, not legal standards or probability estimates.
rubric.threshold_note: 100 is the internal floor only if every limb is at least 25/50. A total of 100 or more does not pass if any limb is below 25. 200/200 means every limb is at 50: twice the internal floor on each limb, the owner's double-lock target. It is not 200% statistical certainty and cannot guarantee a court outcome.
rubric.progress: Threshold progress percentage = the weakest limb divided by 25, capped at 100%. This deliberately prevents strong evidence on one element compensating for a missing essential element. The total score out of 200 is shown as a separate evidence index.
rubric.order: Score high to low; ties by materiality (limb b), process integrity (limb c), then proof quality (limb d).
rubric.reasonable_diligence: Reasonable diligence is not scored as a core limb of a freestanding Takhar fraud action. Takhar rejects a general diligence prerequisite where fraud was not alleged at the original trial, subject to abuse-of-process considerations in the particular case. Diligence remains tracked separately for procedural-route analysis and any ordinary fresh-evidence route.

source.note: All 15 leads have been recalibrated against the fraud/materiality/process-integrity/proof rubric. Their component scores remain provisional desk assessments; source records must be read and authenticated. The case-wide CPR 52.30 route gate remains unresolved and blocks filing.

quarantine_note: Kissed-frog items remain quarantined and are not scored. Post-July 1987 archaeology and later records-disclosure events are not treated as causes of the July 1987 judgment without primary evidence of pre-judgment knowledge and material deception.

rows.title: The licence letters rejected in writing?
rows.what: The decisive finding was that Mary (Nancy) Williams never told BP she rejected the 1974 letters ('she did not, however, do that'). A written rejection, if BP held one while its case said there was none, would go to the heart of the decision.

why.a: No evidence yet that BP possessed a written rejection or knowingly concealed one. The lead identifies what a future record might prove, not proof of deliberate dishonesty now.
why.b: The court wrote that the result 'may' have been different had she plainly told BP she did not accept the letters.
why.c: Potentially central if an authenticated rejection was held by BP and withheld or the court was misled about its existence. No such record has been found, so critical corruption of the litigation process is not yet demonstrated.
why.d: No communication to BP after 4 November 1974 has been found.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Find and authenticate a contemporaneous written rejection, or BP/solicitor file material recording it; identify who knew of it, whether it was withheld or represented as absent, the disclosure history, and exactly what the 1987 court was told.

rows.title: 31 October 1974 licence letters: could BP Properties give a licence?
rows.what: The Court of Appeal answered the 'wrong company' point from the letters' own words that BP Properties Ltd 'had agreed to buy'. Completion came only in May 1975, and HM Land Registry's file adds a plan to that sale dated 23 February 1975.

why.a: The letters say BP Properties had agreed to buy. No record yet shows that the writers knew this was false or misleading when they said it.
why.b: The whole result rests on the licence of BP Properties Ltd: 'from the time of her receipt of the letters, Mrs Buckler was in possession ... by the licence of BP Properties Ltd'.
why.c: This could matter only if primary evidence showed that the writers knowingly misstated BP Properties' status and that the court was thereby misled on the point that determined the licence finding. Neither element is proved on the present record.
why.d: Catalogue entries only; the conveyance and any recital of the contract date are unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Read the 1975 conveyance, contract and contemporaneous BP Properties file. Look for instructions or correspondence showing the writers knew the asserted purchase status was false, and link that statement to the court's licence finding.

rows.title: The 31 December 1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract missing from the title files
rows.what: In September 1974 BP Pension Trust obtained leave to enforce the 1962 possession order 'as successors in title to Western Ground Rents'. The 1969 conveyance from Western Ground Rents is not among the documents lodged on either first-registration file.

why.a: No primary record presently shows that BP Pension Trust or its predecessor knowingly misstated succession to the 1962 judgment.
why.b: The court held that enforcement of the 1962 judgment 'was still open to the landlords at October 31 1974'. Only the judgment creditor or its successor could enforce it.
why.c: A missing deed or incomplete title file is not itself a corrupted process. This would need proof that a party knowingly misstated the successor's rights, that the court was deceived, and that the misstatement materially affected its decision.
why.d: Absence from a list of lodged documents does not prove the deed did not exist; the deed itself is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Obtain the 1969 conveyance and the 1974 affidavit for leave. Establish whether BP knowingly misstated succession to the 1962 judgment, whether the court was deceived, and whether that assertion was material to the 1987 decision.

rows.title: 1982–83 first registration of the farmhouse without the occupier
rows.what: The farmhouse was registered separately (title WA240304, application on Form 1C, register edition 23 February 1983) while BP's own 1974 action against the occupier, Mary (Nancy) Williams, had never been finally heard.

why.a: The application and statutory declaration have not yet been read. No current record shows that the applicant or its agent knowingly made a false statement about occupation.
why.b: The Court of Appeal held that any title she had acquired would have been an overriding interest binding the registration, so the registration date was not why she lost.
why.c: A registration irregularity alone does not show that the 1987 appeal process was corrupted. The Court of Appeal treated an accrued overriding interest as binding on registration; no evidence links the application to the reasoning that decided the appeal.
why.d: An official anomaly; the declaration itself is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Read the complete Form 1C, statutory declaration, requisitions and service record. A route to a fraud ground would require a knowingly false statement attributable to the successful party and proof that the court relied on it materially.
rows.status: Open: HM Land Registry request pending

rows.title: 1877 Bute–Thomas agreement and the 1928 last rent
rows.what: Our case: the farmhouse plot left the Bute estate under an 1877 arrangement with Daniel Thomas & Son, with rent ending in 1928. If so, the farmhouse lay outside the 1916 and 1949 tenancies and the 1938 conveyance, and the paper title the court relied on would fail for it.

why.a: The 1877 agreement and later rent history may challenge the title narrative, but they do not yet show that anyone knowingly concealed the arrangement or lied to the court.
why.b: The court started from BP's 'paper title to the farm' and a 1916 tenancy of 'the whole of the farm'.
why.c: A competing title theory, even if ultimately correct, is not fraud. The process-integrity case requires proof that a party knowingly concealed the 1877 arrangement or made a material false representation to the court and that this affected the judgment.
why.d: The 1877 agreement, plan and 1928 receipt are unread originals.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Produce the 1877 agreement and plan, 1928 receipt and 1938 conveyance with plans; then identify contemporaneous material showing deliberate concealment or a knowingly false title/tenancy assertion actually relied on by the court.

rows.title: 1975 conveyance reservations and 'safeguard your future occupation'
rows.what: The 1974 letters gave the sale to BP Properties as 'the only way' to 'safeguard your future occupation'. The 23 May 1975 conveyance, as entered on the register, kept development rights over the farmhouse plot.

why.a: The wording of the 1974 letters and the later conveyance reservations raise a question about purpose, but do not prove conscious and deliberate dishonesty.
why.b: The court decided the letters' legal effect; the writer's motive played no part in that reasoning.
why.c: The conveyance may expose a factual inconsistency, but the current record does not show a knowingly false representation to the court or that such a representation was an operative cause of the licence decision.
why.d: A register view, not an official copy; the deed is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Read the official 1975 conveyance, plan, contract and drafting file. Identify any knowingly false representation to the 1987 court and show that it was an operative cause of the licence decision.

rows.title: 2 February 1987: the two titles merged while the appeal was pending
rows.what: HM Land Registry merged the farmhouse title (WA240304) into the main title (WA231076) on 2 February 1987, while the appeal was before the Court of Appeal.

why.a: The timing of the amalgamation raises a question, but the applicant, purpose and knowledge are not established. Timing alone is not deliberate dishonesty.
why.b: The court's description of the registration matches the register as merged, but it held the registration date was not why the occupier lost.
why.c: An administrative amalgamation during the appeal, without proof of concealment or reliance by the court, does not show that the appeal process was critically undermined. The judgment treated the registration date as non-determinative.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Obtain the full amalgamation application, plan and correspondence. It would need to show more than an administrative change: deliberate concealment or misrepresentation, court reliance and a powerful link to the appeal result.
rows.status: Open: record requested (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: Title papers taken from the blanket box (1950)
rows.what: The judgment records that documents proving title were 'never produced'. A typed statement from about 1974 records that in June 1950 a Penarth estate agent had the family's papers taken from a blanket box.

why.a: The account is second-hand and does not yet link the agent to Western Ground Rents, BP or a deliberate concealment of title papers.
why.b: The missing papers appear only in the judgment's background; the decision turned on the 1974 letters.
why.c: The family account may explain a title-record gap, but it does not yet connect a dishonest act by the successful party to the court's decision. Its present form is too indirect to show critical process corruption.
why.d: An unsigned, undated typed copy with its last page missing.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Locate the original statement, establish its author and provenance, identify the agent independently, and find records linking that agent to BP/WGR and to deliberate concealment that materially misled the court.

rows.title: Village green VG41 (1970)
rows.what: Land was registered as village green VG41 in 1970 by Glamorgan County Council, whose own planning committee had heard Mary (Nancy) Williams object in 1958 that family land had been 'wrongfully appropriated'.

why.a: No village-green application has been read; the legislation also permitted registration by the authority. No knowingly false statement is identified.
why.b: The judgment does not mention the green, so it cannot have caused the 1987 decision. A separate route (correcting the register), not a reopening ground.
why.c: This concerns a separate village-green registration route. The 1987 judgment did not rely on VG41, so the current material cannot show that the appeal process was corrupted.
why.d: A newspaper report of her words; the VG41 file is unread.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Keep this on its separate register-correction route. It should enter the reopening score only if primary evidence proves deliberate false evidence or concealment actually relied on in the 1987 judgment.

rows.title: Letters addressed to 'Mrs Buckler'
rows.what: The 1974 letters were addressed to 'Mrs Buckler', not Mary (Nancy) Williams.

why.a: The letters addressed to Mrs Buckler were before the court. No separate concealed fact or knowingly false statement is identified by this lead.
why.c: The letters were already before the 1987 court. Without proof of a concealed fact or false representation not addressed by the court, this does not presently show a corrupted process.

rows.what_would_raise_it: No present uplift is identified. Reassess only if a distinct, previously concealed fact or knowingly false representation emerges and can be tied to the court's reasoning.

rows.title: Missing public records and 'no records found' answers
rows.what: The 1988 demolition, Cadw's missing 1988 file and answers that records 'would have been destroyed'. Limitation Act 1980 s.32 postpones time where facts were deliberately concealed.

why.a: Different modern explanations for missing records do not establish that anyone deliberately concealed material from the 1987 court.
why.b: All of this happened after the July 1987 judgment, so it cannot have caused it.
why.c: The demolition, later file-loss explanations and modern disclosure replies post-date the July 1987 judgment. They cannot have caused or corrupted that decision and belong in a separate records-accountability track.
why.d: Not yet assessable: no destruction log has been read.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Do not raise the 1987 reopening score with post-judgment record loss alone. Keep destruction logs, retention schedules and disclosure answers in the separate records/limitation analysis.
rows.status: Parked as a reopening ground: after 1987

rows.title: The May 1939 letting: is the John Williams signature his?
rows.what: A May 1939 agreement by which Western Ground Rents let 5.30 acres of pasture to John Williams the younger, signed before a bank cashier. Our case asks whether the signature is his.

why.a: The signature question remains untested. There is no handwriting opinion, proof of forgery or evidence that a responsible party knowingly used a false signature.
why.b: The 1987 judgment does not mention the 1939 letting. It rested on the 1916 tenancy, the 1949 surrender and re-grant, and the 31 October 1974 letters.
why.c: Even a proved signature anomaly in the 1939 letting would need to be tied to a knowingly false case advanced to the 1987 court and shown to have affected its reasoning. No such link is presently identified.
why.d: Nothing a court could weigh yet: one photograph, no specimens, no examiner.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Obtain the complete DBDT123/7 agreement and dated comparison signatures, then an independent handwriting report. Even a proved forgery needs proof of knowing use, court deception and materiality to the 1987 decision.

rows.title: The 29 March 1961 woodland deed
rows.what: A deed between Western Ground Rents, South Western Brick & Tile and Cardiff City Corporation, known only from its recital on the woodland title WA735527.

why.a: The woodland deed and plan have not been read. No deliberate false statement or concealment connected with the 1987 decision is presently identified.
why.b: The 1987 judgment does not rely on it, and the appeal concerned only the farmhouse and garden.
why.c: The woodland deed may affect parcel analysis, but no dishonest conduct or court deception connected with the 1987 decision is presently identified.
why.d: No copy, image or transcript held.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Order the 1961 deed and plan, map the parcels precisely, and identify any knowingly false representation about them that was made to and materially relied on by the 1987 court.
rows.status: Open: deed orderable (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: July 1955: possession taken beyond the order
rows.what: Our case asks whether the 1955 Order 14 possession order reached all the ground that was taken on 4 July 1955.

why.a: The current record does not show that anyone knowingly misrepresented the scope of the 1955 order to the 1987 court.
why.b: The judgment records possession taken in 1955 of all parts of the farm except the farmhouse and garden, and the 1987 appeal concerned only the farmhouse and garden.
why.c: The recorded 1955 possession event excluded the farmhouse and garden, while the 1987 appeal concerned those premises. The current material does not show a powerful probability of a different appeal decision.

rows.what_would_raise_it: No present uplift is identified. Any further work would need to connect the alleged overreach to the farmhouse/garden issue actually decided in 1987 and to a deliberate false representation to the court.
rows.status: Open: records not located (Mr Wolf seed score)

rows.title: Burials under the farmhouse plot known before 1987?
rows.what: Was knowledge of the burials found under the farm (1,026 recorded in 1994) held before the 1986–87 trial and kept from the court?

why.a: No pre-1987 record presently shows plot-specific knowledge of burials, still less deliberate concealment from the court.
why.b: What lay underground has no bearing on whether the 1974 letters turned possession into permission.
why.c: No pre-July 1987 evidence of knowledge has been identified. Later archaeology cannot show that the 1987 court was deceived or that the decision-making process was critically undermined.
why.d: Credible sources, but they would not have influenced the decision.

rows.what_would_raise_it: Only a primary record dated before July 1987 showing plot-specific knowledge could reopen this lead; it would still need proof of deliberate concealment from the court and material effect on the issue decided.

route_gate.governing_route: The 1987 decision is a final Court of Appeal determination. The current procedural route must be advised, not assumed.

requirements: Reopening must be necessary to avoid real injustice.
Circumstances must be exceptional and make reopening appropriate.
There must be no alternative effective remedy.
authorities: Goring-on-Thames Parish Council v South Oxfordshire DC [2018] EWCA Civ 860
Wingfield v Canterbury City Council [2020] EWCA Civ 1588
cpr_52_30.further_requirements: The earlier process must have been critically undermined; there must be a powerful probability of significant injustice and a powerful probability the decision would have been different if integrity had not been undermined. Mere fresh evidence or an arguably wrong result is insufficient.

takhar_action.requirements: A freestanding action to set aside a judgment for fraud is a distinct cause of action, not the same as reopening the appeal. It requires conscious and deliberate dishonesty attributable to the successful party (or a person for whom it is responsible), deception of the court, and materiality: the fraud must be an operative cause and would have changed how the original court approached the evidence.
takhar_action.diligence: A reasonable-diligence bar is not a general element of this cause of action; deliberate non-investigation of a known suspicion may still be relevant to abuse of process.

unresolved_questions: Which procedural route is legally available for this 1987 final appeal, and in what court?
Could a freestanding Takhar fraud action be an alternative effective remedy, affecting CPR 52.30?
Can the no-alternative-effective-remedy condition be proved?
Do limitation, deliberate-concealment postponement, standing, parties, service and other procedural requirements permit the proposed route?
Has independent counsel reviewed the pleaded fraud particulars and evidence bundle?
route_gate.hard_stop: No individual lead score, even 200/200, authorises filing while the case-wide procedural route remains unresolved.
